claim: Rubella virus predominantly infects microglia in human brain slices from mid-gestation samples.
source: At 72 hr post-infection, immunostaining for the RV capsid protein revealed numerous cells positive for the RV antigen, of which >90% were co-labeled with the microglia marker Iba1 (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing co-localization of RV capsid with Iba1 marker in brain slices, with quantification showing 764/819 (93.3%) of RV+ cells were microglia.

claim: RV-GFP expresses GFP predominantly in microglia in human primary brain slices.
source: In human primary brain slices infected with RV-GFP, GFP expression was detected predominantly in microglia, confirming the production of RV proteins inside this cell type (Figure 1F) consistent with the wild type M33 RV.
evidence: Demonstrated by GFP fluorescence co-localizing with Iba1-positive microglia in brain slices infected with RV-GFP construct.

claim: Microglia represent only 1–5% of the cells of the human developing brain.
source: Such specificity of RV for microglia in this model is striking given that microglia represent only 1–5% of the cells of the human developing brain (Menassa et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature on microglia composition in developing brain.

claim: RV infection of purified microglia monoculture is negligible.
source: Surprisingly, RV infection of the microglia monoculture was negligible (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunostaining showing less than 2% of microglia were positive for RV capsid in pure microglial cultures.

claim: Co-culture of microglia with neurons, glial cells, or mixed brain cells restores RV infection of microglia.
source: Microglia were co-cultured with either neuronally enriched cultures (sorted with PSA-NCAM magnetic beads) or the glial component (flow-through that was depleted of both the CD11b-positive microglia cells and the PSA-NCAM-positive population). Both conditions together with mixed brain cells (flow-through from CD11b-depleted fraction; FT) successfully restored infection (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing up to 60% of microglia had RV capsid immunopositivity when different cell fractions were added to the culture.

claim: In pure microglial cultures, less than 2% of microglia were positive for RV capsid, but when different cell fractions were added, up to 60% of microglia had RV capsid immunopositivity.
source: In the pure microglial cultures, less than 2% of microglia were positive for RV capsid by immunostaining, but when different cell fractions were added to the culture (neuronal, glial, or mixed cultures), up to 60% of microglia had RV capsid immunopositivity (Figure 2F).
evidence: Quantitative immunostaining data comparing RV capsid positivity across different culture conditions.

claim: Microglia represented the main cell type infected with RV in mixed co-cultures.
source: Similar to the cortical brain slices, microglia represented the main cell type infected with RV in the mixed co-cultures (Figure 2G).
evidence: Quantification showing high proportion of RV+ cells are microglia in mixed cultures.

claim: RV titering experiments failed to detect significant production of newly released virions in microglia co-cultures.
source: Despite RV capsid co-localizing with microglia cells and GFP protein being produced from RV-GFP in microglia, RV titering experiments failed to detect significant production of newly released virions in microglia co-cultures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Viral titer measurements showing viral titer falls below detection levels after several days of infection in primary microglia co-cultures.

claim: Both the presence of other cell types in the same well (co-culture) and the media exchange between transwell chambers restored infection in microglia.
source: Both the presence of other cell types in the same well (co-culture) and the media exchange between the two chambers (transwell) restored infection in microglia (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Immunostaining data from transwell experiments showing RV capsid immunopositivity in microglia under both co-culture and transwell conditions.

claim: RV capsid immunostaining in microglia cannot be explained by phagocytosis of other infected cells.
source: Together, these results suggest that RV capsid immunostaining cannot be explained by phagocytosis of other infected cells, but it is possible that infection of microglia is influenced by diffusible factors from other cell populations found in the tissue microenvironment.
evidence: Inferred from transwell experiments where microglia and other cell types are separated by a semi-permeable membrane but infection is still restored.

claim: Infection of microglia is influenced by diffusible factors from other cell populations found in the tissue microenvironment.
source: Together, these results suggest that RV capsid immunostaining cannot be explained by phagocytosis of other infected cells, but it is possible that infection of microglia is influenced by diffusible factors from other cell populations found in the tissue microenvironment.
evidence: Inferred from transwell experiments showing media exchange alone can restore infection without direct cell-cell contact.

claim: In organoids with engrafted primary microglia subsequently exposed to RV, RV capsid was detected in microglia, but not in other cell types, at both 72 hr and 2 weeks timepoints.
source: In organoids with engrafted primary microglia subsequently exposed to RV, immunostaining revealed RV capsid in microglia, similar to primary tissue and co-culture experiments. We detected RV capsid in microglia, but not in other cell types, in both timepoints, suggesting that microglia remain the main cell population that harbors viral infection (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: Immunofluorescence images showing RV capsid co-localization with Iba1-positive microglia at 72 hr and 2 weeks post-exposure.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing of neuroimmune organoids at 72 hr after RV exposure revealed approximately 11,000 cells passing filtering criteria.
source: After processing for scRNAseq, cells with fewer than 500 detected genes and/or more than 20% mitochondrial genes were removed from the analysis. Ribosomal transcripts and pseudogenes were excluded. Approximately 11,000 cells passed filtering criteria (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C), revealing the expected major cell populations of the human developing brain (Nowakowski et al., 2017), including radial glia cells, immature and mature neurons, and astrocytes (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Quality control metrics and cell counts from scRNAseq analysis.

claim: scRNAseq analysis revealed expected major cell populations of the human developing brain, including radial glia cells, immature and mature neurons, and astrocytes.
source: Approximately 11,000 cells passed filtering criteria (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C), revealing the expected major cell populations of the human developing brain (Nowakowski et al., 2017), including radial glia cells, immature and mature neurons, and astrocytes (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: UMAP clustering and marker gene expression analysis identifying distinct cell populations.

claim: A separate microglia cluster was not identified in the scRNAseq analysis.
source: A separate microglia cluster was not identified.
evidence: Absence of distinct microglia cluster in UMAP analysis and lack of canonical microglia marker P2RY12 detection.

claim: The apparent lack of microglia in scRNAseq data is attributed to both the small starting population and loss due to cell dissociation during processing.
source: We attribute the apparent lack of microglia to both the small starting population and loss due to cell dissociation during processing for scRNAseq.
evidence: Inference based on known technical limitations of scRNAseq processing and the small proportion of microglia in organoids.

claim: Exposure of organoids to RV resulted in significant transcriptomic differences including genes involved in the interferon signaling pathway and its response.
source: However, exposure of organoids to RV resulted in significant transcriptomic differences including genes involved in the interferon signaling pathway and its response (IFI27, IFI6, IFITM3) (HLA-A [Campbell et al., 1986; Keskinen et al., 1997] and BST2 [Holmgren et al., 2015]) (cluster 1, Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Differential gene expression analysis from scRNAseq data showing upregulation of interferon-related genes in RV-exposed organoids.

claim: The majority of cells in cluster 1 came from RV-exposed organoids.
source: The majority of cells in cluster 1 came from RV-exposed organoids (Figure 5D).
evidence: UMAP visualization showing distribution of cells by treatment condition.

claim: While genes involved in the interferon response showed increased expression in organoids both with and without microglia, the magnitude of their upregulation was lower among cells in microglia-containing organoids.
source: While genes involved in the interferon response showed increased expression in organoids both with and without microglia, the magnitude of their upregulation was lower among cells in microglia-containing organoids (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: Comparative gene expression analysis showing differential IFITM3 expression levels between organoids with and without microglia.

claim: IFITM3 protein expression was higher in organoids with microglia exposed to RV compared to organoids with microglia exposed to heat-inactivated RV at 72 hr post-exposure.
source: We confirmed higher expression levels of IFITM3 protein in organoids with microglia exposed to RV in comparison to organoids with microglia exposed to heat-inactivated RV at 72 hr post-exposure (Figure 5G–H), while the overall cell numbers were not changed in either condition (Figure 5I).
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification showing statistically significant difference in IFITM3 intensity (p-value = 0.04).

claim: Overall cell numbers were not changed between RV-exposed and control organoids with microglia.
source: We confirmed higher expression levels of IFITM3 protein in organoids with microglia exposed to RV in comparison to organoids with microglia exposed to heat-inactivated RV at 72 hr post-exposure (Figure 5G–H), while the overall cell numbers were not changed in either condition (Figure 5I).
evidence: DAPI quantification showing no significant difference in cell numbers (p-value = 0.22).

claim: Radial glia and dividing cells had a greater transcriptomic response to RV exposure compared to neurons, both with and without microglia.
source: Radial glia and dividing cells had a greater transcriptomic response to RV exposure as compared to neurons, both with and without microglia (Figure 6A).
evidence: Differential gene expression analysis showing number of DEGs across different cell types.

claim: Cells captured from microglia-containing organoids showed fewer differentially expressed genes in response to RV in each of the major cell classes compared to organoids that did not contain microglia.
source: Cells captured from microglia-containing organoids showed fewer differentially expressed genes in response to RV in each of the major cell classes compared to organoids that did not contain microglia (Figure 6A, top vs bottom panel), with radial glia and neurons reaching statistically significant levels (p-values shown on the right side of the panel) and neural progenitor cells showing the overall trend without reaching statistical significance.
evidence: Statistical comparison of DEG numbers between conditions using Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.

claim: Nuclear factor I genes NFIB and NFIA were specifically downregulated in the presence of RV in organoids without microglia.
source: One gene family that was specifically downregulated in the presence of RV in organoids without microglia included nuclear factor I – NFIB and NFIA (Figure 6A, Figure 5—source data 2) – two genes that form heterodimers in vivo and are associated with induction of gliogenesis (Tchieu et al., 2019) in embryonic brain development.
evidence: Differential gene expression data showing downregulation of NFIB and NFIA in RV-exposed organoids without microglia.

claim: NFIB and NFIA form heterodimers in vivo and are associated with induction of gliogenesis in embryonic brain development.
source: One gene family that was specifically downregulated in the presence of RV in organoids without microglia included nuclear factor I – NFIB and NFIA (Figure 6A, Figure 5—source data 2) – two genes that form heterodimers in vivo and are associated with induction of gliogenesis (Tchieu et al., 2019) in embryonic brain development.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature on NFIB/NFIA function.

claim: Early disruption in the function of either NFIB or NFIA is associated with neurodevelopmental deficits and perinatal mortality in mice.
source: Early disruption in the function of either gene is associated with neurodevelopmental deficits and perinatal mortality in mice (das Neves et al., 1999; Steele-Perkins et al., 2005) and with intellectual disability in humans (Schanze et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published mouse studies.

claim: Disruption of NFIB or NFIA function is associated with intellectual disability in humans.
source: Early disruption in the function of either gene is associated with neurodevelopmental deficits and perinatal mortality in mice (das Neves et al., 1999; Steele-Perkins et al., 2005) and with intellectual disability in humans (Schanze et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published human genetic studies.

claim: NOVA1 expression levels were affected both by the presence of microglia and by RV exposure.
source: Genes with expression levels affected both by the presence of microglia and by RV exposure included NOVA alternative splicing regulator 1 (NOVA1) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Violin plot showing NOVA1 expression across different conditions and cell types.

claim: NOVA1 is a master regulator of alternative splicing in the central nervous system with potential links to neurological diseases.
source: NOVA1 is a master regulator of alternative splicing (Zhang et al., 2010) in the central nervous system with potential links to neurological diseases (Parikshak et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature on NOVA1 function.

claim: A statistically significant decrease of NOVA1+ intermediate progenitor cells was detected in response to RV exposure in neuroimmune organoids at 2 weeks.
source: We detected a statistically significant decrease of NOVA1+ IPCs in response to RV exposure (Figure 6E).
evidence: Immunostaining quantification showing significant reduction (p-value = 0.0042) in NOVA1+/EOMES+ cells.

claim: Numbers of NOVA1+ neurons showed a trend toward reduction in RV-exposed organoids, but it did not reach statistical significance.
source: Numbers of NOVA1+ neurons also had a trend toward reduction (Figure 6D); however, it did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: Immunostaining quantification showing trend but non-significant p-value (p-value = 0.088).

claim: Lower numbers of neurons were detected in organoids after RV exposure at 2 weeks.
source: Concurrently with reduction of NOVA1+ cells, we detected lower numbers of neurons (Figure 6F), but not IPCs (Figure 6G), in organoids after RV exposure.
evidence: Immunostaining quantification showing significant reduction in NeuN+ neurons per organoid area (p-value = 0.0004).

claim: Numbers of intermediate progenitor cells were not significantly changed in organoids after RV exposure at 2 weeks.
source: Concurrently with reduction of NOVA1+ cells, we detected lower numbers of neurons (Figure 6F), but not IPCs (Figure 6G), in organoids after RV exposure.
evidence: Immunostaining quantification showing no significant difference in EOMES+ cells per organoid area (p-value = 0.86).

claim: Rubella virus is an enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus of the family Matonaviridae restricted to human transmission.
source: This is true even for well-studied pathogens like rubella virus (RV), which is an enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus of the family Matonaviridae restricted to human transmission.
evidence: Statement of established virological classification.

claim: Infection with RV typically causes a mild, self-limiting illness with a characteristic rash during childhood, often referred to as 'German measles'.
source: Infection with RV typically causes a mild, self-limiting illness with a characteristic rash during childhood, often referred to as 'German measles'.
evidence: Statement of established clinical presentation.

claim: Infection during pregnancy can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or a range of birth defects including congenital rubella syndrome (CRS).
source: However, infection during pregnancy can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or a range of birth defects including congenital rubella syndrome (CRS).
evidence: Statement of established clinical outcomes.

claim: The sequelae of congenital RV infection were first recognized in 1941.
source: The sequelae of congenital RV infection were first recognized in 1941 and although the first RV vaccines were licensed in 1969, an estimated 105,000 infants with CRS were born each year worldwide as of 2010 (Vynnycky et al., 2016).
evidence: Historical fact supported by citation.

claim: The first RV vaccines were licensed in 1969.
source: The sequelae of congenital RV infection were first recognized in 1941 and although the first RV vaccines were licensed in 1969, an estimated 105,000 infants with CRS were born each year worldwide as of 2010 (Vynnycky et al., 2016).
evidence: Historical fact supported by citation.

claim: An estimated 105,000 infants with CRS were born each year worldwide as of 2010.
source: The sequelae of congenital RV infection were first recognized in 1941 and although the first RV vaccines were licensed in 1969, an estimated 105,000 infants with CRS were born each year worldwide as of 2010 (Vynnycky et al., 2016).
evidence: Epidemiological estimate supported by citation.

claim: As of 2019, RV-containing vaccine coverage remains incomplete and inconsistent, with ongoing endemic transmission and reporting gaps primarily in the African, Eastern Mediterranean, and South-East Asian World Health Organization Regions.
source: As of 2019, RV-containing vaccine coverage remains incomplete and inconsistent, with ongoing endemic transmission and reporting gaps primarily in the African, Eastern Mediterranean, and South-East Asian World Health Organization Regions (World Health Organization, 2020).
evidence: Epidemiological data supported by WHO citation.

claim: Outbreaks in Japan and China in 2013–14 and 2018–19 caused a twofold increase in reported rubella cases worldwide (26,033 total cases in 2018 vs 49,179 cases in 2019).
source: Countries with RV-containing vaccine programs also remain susceptible to outbreaks, such as Japan and China, where outbreaks in 2013–14 and 2018–19 caused a twofold increase in reported rubella cases worldwide (26,033 total cases in 2018 vs 49,179 cases in 2019) (Plotkin, 2021) and included CRS the following year (423 total cases worldwide in 2019 vs 1252 cases in 2020) (World Health Organization, 2022).
evidence: Epidemiological data supported by citations.

claim: CRS cases increased from 423 total cases worldwide in 2019 to 1252 cases in 2020.
source: Countries with RV-containing vaccine programs also remain susceptible to outbreaks, such as Japan and China, where outbreaks in 2013–14 and 2018–19 caused a twofold increase in reported rubella cases worldwide (26,033 total cases in 2018 vs 49,179 cases in 2019) (Plotkin, 2021) and included CRS the following year (423 total cases worldwide in 2019 vs 1252 cases in 2020) (World Health Organization, 2022).
evidence: Epidemiological data supported by WHO citation.

claim: The most common features of CRS are congenital cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and cardiac defects.
source: The most common features of CRS are congenital cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and cardiac defects (Banatvala and Brown, 2004).
evidence: Clinical features supported by citation.

claim: Microcephaly, developmental delay and autism, and schizophrenia spectrum disorders are associated with congenital rubella syndrome.
source: In addition, microcephaly (Munro et al., 1987), developmental delay and autism (Chess, 1977), and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (Brown et al., 2001) are associated with the syndrome, but the pathophysiology of these neurological complications is not well described.
evidence: Clinical associations supported by multiple citations.

claim: Initial RV infection in the lymphoid tissues of the nasopharynx and upper respiratory tract leads to systemic viremia, with virus spread across the placenta and into nearly all fetal organs on post-mortem examination, primarily via infected mononuclear cells.
source: Initial infection in the lymphoid tissues of the nasopharynx and upper respiratory tract leads to systemic viremia, with virus spread across the placenta and into nearly all fetal organs on post-mortem examination, primarily via infected mononuclear cells (Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: Pathophysiological mechanism supported by citation.

claim: RV was isolated from cerebrospinal fluid and brain tissue of fetuses and infants with CRS in studies from the 1960s.
source: As for the fetal nervous system, RV was isolated from cerebrospinal fluid and brain tissue of fetuses and infants with CRS in studies from the 1960s (Bellanti et al., 1965; Esterly and Oppenheimer, 1967; Korones, 1965; Monif et al., 1965).
evidence: Historical findings supported by multiple citations.

claim: Autopsies in the 1960s revealed nonspecific gliosis and cerebral vessel degeneration in CRS cases.
source: Autopsies in that early era revealed nonspecific gliosis and cerebral vessel degeneration (Rorke and Spiro, 1967).
evidence: Pathological findings supported by citation.

claim: In limited pathology specimens from more recent outbreaks, RV RNA and antigens were identified in rare cells in the cortex and cerebellum presumed to be 'nerve cells' and neural progenitor cells.
source: In limited pathology specimens from more recent outbreaks, RV RNA and antigens were identified in rare cells in the cortex and cerebellum presumed to be 'nerve cells' and neural progenitor cells (Lazar et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2015).
evidence: Pathological findings supported by citations.

claim: Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) has been proposed as a cellular receptor for RV.
source: To complicate the matter, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) has been proposed as a cellular receptor for RV (Cong et al., 2011), but it is exclusively expressed in oligodendrocytes in the human brain and therefore cannot explain infection in other cell populations.
evidence: Proposed mechanism supported by citation.

claim: MOG is exclusively expressed in oligodendrocytes in the human brain and therefore cannot explain RV infection in other cell populations.
source: To complicate the matter, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) has been proposed as a cellular receptor for RV (Cong et al., 2011), but it is exclusively expressed in oligodendrocytes in the human brain and therefore cannot explain infection in other cell populations.
evidence: Inference based on known MOG expression pattern and observed infection in non-oligodendrocyte cells.

claim: RV tropism for microglia is consistent with RV tropism for monocytes in the periphery.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in the developing brain RV predominantly infects microglia, the resident macrophage population. This finding is consistent with RV tropism for monocytes in the periphery (Perelygina et al., 2021; van der Logt et al., 1980), and adds new information to the limited understanding of RV infection in the central nervous system.
evidence: Comparison to published findings on peripheral RV tropism.

claim: Tropism for microglia raises questions about how and where RV persists in CRS, perhaps in brain tissue during the extended period of viral shedding, similar to other relatively immuno-privileged sites such as the eye.
source: Tropism for microglia raises interesting questions about how and where RV persists in CRS, perhaps in brain tissue during the extended period of viral shedding, similar to other relatively immuno-privileged sites such as the eye (Doan et al., 2016; Sugishita et al., 2016).
evidence: Speculation based on observed tropism and comparison to other sites of persistence.

claim: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 and Zika virus target microglia directly.
source: Our findings also help contextualize CRS in comparison to congenital infections by other neurotropic viruses: human immunodeficiency virus type 1 and Zika virus, which target microglia directly; herpes simplex virus, which replicates poorly in microglia with cytopathic effect; and human cytomegalovirus, which causes microglia to produce antiviral cytokines without productive infection or cytopathic effect (Lum et al., 2017; Retallack et al., 2016; Rock et al., 2004).
evidence: Comparison to other viruses supported by citations.

claim: Herpes simplex virus replicates poorly in microglia with cytopathic effect.
source: Our findings also help contextualize CRS in comparison to congenital infections by other neurotropic viruses: human immunodeficiency virus type 1 and Zika virus, which target microglia directly; herpes simplex virus, which replicates poorly in microglia with cytopathic effect; and human cytomegalovirus, which causes microglia to produce antiviral cytokines without productive infection or cytopathic effect (Lum et al., 2017; Retallack et al., 2016; Rock et al., 2004).
evidence: Comparison to other viruses supported by citations.

claim: Human cytomegalovirus causes microglia to produce antiviral cytokines without productive infection or cytopathic effect.
source: Our findings also help contextualize CRS in comparison to congenital infections by other neurotropic viruses: human immunodeficiency virus type 1 and Zika virus, which target microglia directly; herpes simplex virus, which replicates poorly in microglia with cytopathic effect; and human cytomegalovirus, which causes microglia to produce antiviral cytokines without productive infection or cytopathic effect (Lum et al., 2017; Retallack et al., 2016; Rock et al., 2004).
evidence: Comparison to other viruses supported by citations.

claim: RV elicits a strong interferon response in non-microglial cell types by establishing viral transcription and translation in microglia.
source: Like some of these other viruses, we found that by establishing viral transcription and translation in microglia, RV elicits a strong interferon response in other cell types.
evidence: Inference based on scRNAseq data showing interferon response genes upregulated in non-microglial cells.

claim: The interferon response in neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells can induce molecular and morphological changes associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, including neurite length and gene expression changes associated with schizophrenia and autism.
source: It has been previously shown that the interferon response in neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells can induce molecular and morphological changes associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, including neurite length and gene expression changes associated with schizophrenia and autism (Warre-Cornish et al., 2020).
evidence: Previous findings supported by citation.

claim: The interferon response is associated with pathobiology in a range of congenital infections and interferonopathies.
source: The interferon response is additionally associated with pathobiology in a range of congenital infections and interferonopathies (Crow and Manel, 2015).
evidence: General statement supported by citation.

claim: In organoids where microglia do not develop under standard protocols, the RV-induced interferon response was attenuated in the presence of microglia, suggesting a possible protective role of microglia on other cell types.
source: Furthermore, in our preliminary experiments in organoids, where microglia do not develop under standard protocols, the RV-induced interferon response was attenuated in the presence of microglia, suggesting a possible protective role of microglia on other cell types.
evidence: Inference based on comparative gene expression data showing lower interferon response magnitude in microglia-containing organoids.

claim: Brain organoids do not robustly develop any cells of myeloid origin under standard protocols.
source: Under standard protocols, brain organoids do not robustly develop any cells of myeloid origin, making them a useful reductionist model for investigating the role of immune cells in brain homeostasis and development (Nowakowski and Salama, 2022).
evidence: Statement about organoid characteristics supported by citation.

claim: Membrane phospholipids and glycolipids have been shown to participate in RV viral entry.
source: Indeed, membrane phospholipids and glycolipids have been shown to participate in viral entry (Mastromarino et al., 1990; Otsuki et al., 2018).
evidence: Previous findings supported by citations.

claim: Rare cells expressing the microglia marker AIF1 were present in organoids, but such cells have been previously reported to develop spontaneously in organoids.
source: Rare cells expressing the microglia marker AIF1 (encoding the Iba1 protein) were present, but such cells have been previously reported to develop spontaneously in organoids (He et al., 2022) and the canonical microglia marker P2RY12 was not detected in those cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Observation supported by citation to previous report and marker analysis.

claim: The canonical microglia marker P2RY12 was not detected in AIF1-positive cells in organoids.
source: Rare cells expressing the microglia marker AIF1 (encoding the Iba1 protein) were present, but such cells have been previously reported to develop spontaneously in organoids (He et al., 2022) and the canonical microglia marker P2RY12 was not detected in those cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Gene expression analysis from scRNAseq data.

claim: Transcriptomic consequences of RV exposure are dependent on the presence of microglia in the organoid tissue environment.
source: We show that transcriptomic consequences of RV exposure are dependent on the presence of microglia in the organoid tissue environment, while future studies will be needed to determine the precise mechanisms that mediate this effect.
evidence: Inference based on differential gene expression analysis comparing organoids with and without microglia.

claim: RV-GFP was generated by inserting an sfGFP sequence flanked by Gly-Gly-Ser-Gly-Gly linkers into the non-structural P150 gene.
source: To confirm functional transcription and translation of the viral genome, a new reporter construct of RV designed to express GFP within the non-structural P150 gene was generated (RV-GFP, GenBank Accession OM816675, Figure 1E) and validated by GFP expression in Vero cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of construct generation and validation in Vero cells.

claim: RV-GFP was validated by GFP expression in Vero cells.
source: To confirm functional transcription and translation of the viral genome, a new reporter construct of RV designed to express GFP within the non-structural P150 gene was generated (RV-GFP, GenBank Accession OM816675, Figure 1E) and validated by GFP expression in Vero cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Immunofluorescence showing co-localization of RV capsid and GFP in Vero cells.

claim: Mixed cultures inoculated with lower viral titers had fewer cells with RV capsid immunopositivity overall, but retained a high proportion of infected microglia demonstrating specificity for microglia.
source: Furthermore, mixed cultures inoculated with lower viral titers had fewer cells with RV capsid immunopositivity overall, but retained a high proportion of infected microglia demonstrating specificity for microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Dose-response experiment showing maintained microglia proportion across different viral titers.

claim: No statistically significant difference was detected in RV infectivity in cells cultured with or without microglia when examining non-microglial cells.
source: No statistically significant difference was detected in RV infectivity in cells cultured with or without microglia (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical analysis of RV+ cells that are not microglia across different cell populations.

claim: The p-value between microglia-only and co-culture conditions for RV capsid immunopositivity among microglia was 0.0479.
source: Three fields of view across the same experiment were quantified for each condition and represent technical replicates. Error bars represent SEM. p-value between microglia and co-culture condition is 0.0479. p-value between microglia and transwell condition is 0.0159.
evidence: Statistical test result from quantification of immunostaining data.

claim: The p-value between microglia-only and transwell conditions for RV capsid immunopositivity among microglia was 0.0159.
source: Three fields of view across the same experiment were quantified for each condition and represent technical replicates. Error bars represent SEM. p-value between microglia and co-culture condition is 0.0479. p-value between microglia and transwell condition is 0.0159.
evidence: Statistical test result from quantification of immunostaining data.

claim: Cerebral organoids were generated following previously established protocols at 5 weeks of differentiation when the majority of cell types are present.
source: Brain organoids were generated following previously established protocols (Paşca et al., 2015), and at 5 weeks of differentiation, when the majority of cell types are present in the organoids, mid-gestation primary human microglia were introduced as previously described (Popova et al., 2021).
evidence: Methods description citing established protocols.

claim: Mid-gestation primary human microglia were introduced into organoids at 5 weeks of differentiation as previously described.
source: Brain organoids were generated following previously established protocols (Paşca et al., 2015), and at 5 weeks of differentiation, when the majority of cell types are present in the organoids, mid-gestation primary human microglia were introduced as previously described (Popova et al., 2021).
evidence: Methods description citing established protocol.

claim: Neuroimmune organoids were exposed to RV or heat-inactivated control and cultured for 72 hr or 2 weeks to identify short- and long-term consequences of viral exposure.
source: After allowing microglia to engraft into the organoids, we exposed neuroimmune organoids to RV or heat-inactivated control and cultured them for 72 hr or 2 weeks to identify short- and long-term consequences of the viral exposure (Figure 4A).
evidence: Experimental design description.

claim: Cell cluster annotations were assigned based on combinations of co-expressed cluster marker genes.
source: Cell cluster annotations were assigned based on combinations of co-expressed cluster marker genes, such as FGFBP2 and SOX2 for radial glial cells (clusters 5 and 10), TAGLN3, HES6, NEUROD4 for neural progenitor cells (cluster 7), TUBB2A, TUBB2B, STMN2 for neurons (cluster 2), CLU, PTN, and SPARCL1 for astrocytes (cluster 6), and MKI67, UBE2C, and CENPF for dividing cells (clusters 3 and 4) (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E for individual cluster marker genes, Figure 5—source data 1 for the full list of markers).
evidence: Description of bioinformatic analysis approach for cell type identification.

claim: Cells derived from organoids with and without microglia were present in all clusters.
source: Cells derived from organoids with and without microglia were present in all clusters (Figure 5C).
evidence: UMAP visualization showing distribution of cells by microglia presence across all clusters.

claim: Appreciable numbers of viral transcripts were not recovered in the scRNAseq data.
source: Consistent with the lack of microglia cells in our scRNAseq data, we did not recover appreciable numbers of the viral transcripts.
evidence: Observation from scRNAseq analysis.

claim: HLA-A is involved in interferon signaling.
source: However, exposure of organoids to RV resulted in significant transcriptomic differences including genes involved in the interferon signaling pathway and its response (IFI27, IFI6, IFITM3) (HLA-A [Campbell et al., 1986; Keskinen et al., 1997] and BST2 [Holmgren et al., 2015]) (cluster 1, Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BST2 is involved in interferon response.
source: However, exposure of organoids to RV resulted in significant transcriptomic differences including genes involved in the interferon signaling pathway and its response (IFI27, IFI6, IFITM3) (HLA-A [Campbell et al., 1986; Keskinen et al., 1997] and BST2 [Holmgren et al., 2015]) (cluster 1, Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Radial glia and neurons showed statistically significant reduction in differentially expressed genes in response to RV when microglia were present.
source: Cells captured from microglia-containing organoids showed fewer differentially expressed genes in response to RV in each of the major cell classes compared to organoids that did not contain microglia (Figure 6A, top vs bottom panel), with radial glia and neurons reaching statistically significant levels (p-values shown on the right side of the panel) and neural progenitor cells showing the overall trend without reaching statistical significance.
evidence: Statistical comparison using Kolmogorov-Smirnov test showing p<0.001 for radial glia and p<0.05 for neurons.

claim: Neural progenitor cells showed an overall trend of fewer DEGs in the presence of microglia without reaching statistical significance.
source: Cells captured from microglia-containing organoids showed fewer differentially expressed genes in response to RV in each of the major cell classes compared to organoids that did not contain microglia (Figure 6A, top vs bottom panel), with radial glia and neurons reaching statistically significant levels (p-values shown on the right side of the panel) and neural progenitor cells showing the overall trend without reaching statistical significance.
evidence: Statistical comparison showing trend but non-significant result.

claim: In organoids with microglia, NOVA1 trended toward a decrease in intermediate progenitor cells and neurons.
source: In organoids with microglia, NOVA1 trended toward a decrease in IPCs and neurons (labeled in blue in the panel).
evidence: Volcano plot showing NOVA1 expression changes in different cell types.

claim: Vero cells were obtained from ATCC (CRL-1587).
source: Vero cells were obtained from ATCC (CRL-1587) and maintained in DMEM (Thermo Fisher, 11965-118) with 10% (vol/vol) fetal bovine serum (Thermo Fisher, 10438026), 10 mM HEPES (Thermo Fisher, 15630-080), and 1× penicillin/streptomycin (Thermo Fisher, 10378016).
evidence: Methods description of cell line source.

claim: Cell cultures were routinely checked to be free from mycoplasma.
source: Cell cultures were routinely checked to be free from mycoplasma.
evidence: Quality control statement for cell culture.

claim: Immunofluorescent titering assays yielded titers of 105–106 focus-forming units/ml (ffu/ml) for RV stocks.
source: Immunofluorescent titering assays were performed on Vero cells using anti-RV capsid antibody (ab34749), yielding titers of 105–106 focus-forming units/ml (ffu/ml) for RV stocks.
evidence: Quantitative measurement of viral titer.

claim: All viral stocks were tested to be free from mycoplasma.
source: All viral stocks were tested to be free from mycoplasma.
evidence: Quality control statement for viral stocks.

claim: Deidentified tissue samples were collected with previous patient consent in strict observance of the legal and institutional ethical regulations.
source: Deidentified tissue samples were collected with previous patient consent in strict observance of the legal and institutional ethical regulations.
evidence: Ethics statement for human tissue use.

claim: Protocols related to human iPSCs were approved by the Human Gamete, Embryo, and Stem Cell Research Committee (institutional review board) at the University of California, San Francisco.
source: Protocols related to human iPSCs were approved by the Human Gamete, Embryo, and Stem Cell Research Committee (institutional review board) at the University of California, San Francisco.
evidence: Ethics approval statement for iPSC work.

claim: Primary prenatal brain tissue was dissociated and microglia were purified using MACS kit with CD11b magnetic beads.
source: Prenatal human microglia were purified from primary brain tissue from mid-gestation (gestational week 18–23) samples using MACS kit with CD11b magnetic beads (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-049-601) following the manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: Methods description of cell purification procedure.

claim: Approximately 1×10^6 microglia cells were routinely obtained from a single MACS purification.
source: We routinely obtained 1×106 of microglia cells from a single MACS purification.
evidence: Quantitative yield from purification procedure.

claim: Human iPSC line 'WTC-10' was derived from healthy 30-year-old Japanese male fibroblasts.
source: Human iPSC line 'WTC-10' derived from healthy 30-year-old Japanese male fibroblasts was from the Conklin Lab, UCSF (Bershteyn et al., 2017; Kreitzer et al., 2013).
evidence: Description of cell line source and characteristics.

claim: Human iPSC line '13325' was derived from 9-year-old female fibroblasts originally obtained from Coriell cell repository.
source: Human iPSC line '13325' was derived from 9-year-old female fibroblasts originally obtained from Coriell cell repository.
evidence: Description of cell line source and characteristics.

claim: Human iPSC line '1323-4' was derived from healthy 48-year-old Caucasian female fibroblasts.
source: Human iPSC line '1323-4' derived from healthy 48-year-old Caucasian female fibroblasts (gift from the Conklin Lab, UCSF) was used for immunofluorescence validation analysis as we found that this line generates more reproducible brain organoids.
evidence: Description of cell line source and rationale for use.

claim: Microglia were plated at 1×10^5 cells/well for 2D cultures.
source: Microglia were plated at 1×105 cells/well and maintained in culture media containing 66% (vol/vol) Eagle's basal medium, 25% (vol/vol) HBSS, 2% (vol/vol) B27 (Thermo Fisher, 17504001), 1% N2 supplement (Thermo Fisher, 17502001), 1% penicillin/streptomycin, and GlutaMax (Thermo Fisher) additionally supplemented with 100 ng/ml IL34 (Peprotech, 200-34), 2 ng/ml TGFβ2 (Peprotech,100-35B), and 1× CD lipid concentrate (Thermo Fisher, 11905031) for 5–8 days.
evidence: Methods description of cell culture conditions.

claim: For co-culture experiments, other cell types were cultured with microglia at 5:1 ratio.
source: For co-culture experiments, other cell types were cultured with microglia at 5:1 ratio (1×105 microglia cells for each 5×105 non-microglial cells).
evidence: Methods description of experimental design.

claim: Microglia from mid-gestation cortical tissue were added to organoids at 1×10^5 microglia cells/organoid.
source: Microglia from mid-gestation cortical tissue were MACS-purified and immediately added to organoids between weeks 5 and 6 in six-well plates at 1×105 microglia cells/organoid and kept off the shaker overnight.
evidence: Methods description of microglia transplantation procedure.

claim: Cells cultured in 2D were inoculated with RV at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 2.
source: Cells cultured in 2D were inoculated by adding RV stock virus to culture media in 1:1 dilution (250 µl of media to the equal volume of viral stock, 1.75×105 total ffu/well) to achieve a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 2.
evidence: Methods description of infection protocol.

claim: CellProfiler 3.0 software was used for quantifying cell co-localization with RV capsid in 2D microglia co-cultures.
source: Cell co-localization with the RV capsid was quantified using the CellProfiler 3.0 software (McQuin et al., 2018).
evidence: Methods description citing software used for analysis.

claim: QuPath 0.3.2 was used for organoid immunofluorescence quantifications.
source: For cytoplasmic IFITM3 staining, whole organoid sections were treated as regions of interest and average fluorescence intensity for IFITM3 was normalized to DAPI fluorescence using QuPath 0.3.2.
evidence: Methods description of image analysis software.

claim: Prism 9.3.1 was used for statistical analysis and data plotting.
source: Prism 9.3.1 was used for statistical analysis and data plotting.
evidence: Methods description of statistical software.

claim: Unpaired t-test with assumed Gaussian distribution was used to calculate statistical significance for cell counts.
source: Unpaired t-test with assumed Gaussian distribution of the variants and the same standard deviations were used to calculate statistical significance for cell counts.
evidence: Methods description of statistical test.

claim: Unpaired nonparametric Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was used to compare differentially expressed genes between conditions in organoids.
source: Unpaired nonparametric Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was used to compare differentially expressed genes that reached significance value of p=0.05 between conditions in organoids.
evidence: Methods description of statistical test.

claim: CellRanger 3.0 was used to create a cell by gene matrix from scRNAseq data.
source: CellRanger 3.0 was used to create a cell by gene matrix which was then processed using Solo (Fleming et al., 2019) for doublet detection and removal.
evidence: Methods description citing bioinformatics pipeline.

claim: Solo was used for doublet detection and removal in scRNAseq analysis.
source: CellRanger 3.0 was used to create a cell by gene matrix which was then processed using Solo (Fleming et al., 2019) for doublet detection and removal.
evidence: Methods description citing bioinformatics tool.

claim: A minimum of 1000 genes, 500 UMI counts, and 20% mitochondrial cutoff were used to remove low-quality cells from scRNAseq datasets.
source: A minimum of 1000 genes, 500 UMI counts, and 20% mitochondrial cutoff were used to remove low-quality cells from all datasets.
evidence: Methods description of quality control criteria.

claim: MAST was used on log normalized raw counts for all differential expression tests.
source: MAST (Finak et al., 2015) was used on log normalized raw counts for all differential expression tests.
evidence: Methods description citing statistical tool.

claim: Organoid demultiplexing and doublet filtering was done through deMULTIplex.
source: Organoid demultiplexing and doublet filtering was done through deMULTIplex (McGinnis et al., 2019) (https://github.com/chris-mcginnis-ucsf/MULTI-seq ; McGinnis, 2019).
evidence: Methods description citing bioinformatics tool.

claim: UMAP embeddings and neighbors for Leiden clustering were used for clustering and visualization.
source: Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) (McInnes et al., 2018) embeddings and neighbors for Leiden clustering (Traag et al., 2019) were used for clustering and visualization.
evidence: Methods description citing bioinformatics approaches.

claim: Organoid cells were batch corrected using default parameters of the SCTransform integration workflow.
source: Organoid cells were batch corrected using default parameters of the SCTransform (Hafemeister and Satija, 2019) integration workflow.
evidence: Methods description citing bioinformatics tool.
